historical_evidence.finding: Split-half reliability of Connector teammate-path quality Q_p was low (r=0.215, Spearman-Brown 0.355, ICC 0.216), indicating that most variance is within-player half-to-half and the measure is too unreliable to treat Q_p as a stable scoutable trait.

Validation of ranked playsheet based on H1-to-H2 PPP drops found weak full-rank signal (Spearman rho=-0.0639), but pairwise BEST vs AVOID comparison showed a significant effect; identified risks: leakage, low measurement reliability, small sample, drift.
Initial positive lag-1 PPP effect after star foul was largely driven by free throws (artifact); after excluding free throws the effect disappeared.
PCI's incremental R2 over ORtg was mainly due to leakage tracking DRtg; the offensive-control component added only 0.005 R2, revealing an artifact from construction.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Split-half reliability test for a derived player-level metric (Connector Q_p)
failed_approaches.why: Low measurement reliability (MEASURE_RELIABILITY), leading to untestable conclusion due to high within-player half-to-half variance.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Ranked playsheet prediction using H1-to-H2 PPP changes
failed_approaches.why: Inconclusive due to small sample, measurement noise, and leakage/confounding; Spearman rank correlation not significantly positive.
Initial positive result was artifact from free throws; after proper control, no significant effect; risks included BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, MECHANICAL_FLOOR.
Apparent incremental R2 was leakage tracking DRtg; artifact from construction.

evidence_establishes: Derived half-to-half metrics can suffer from low measurement reliability at the player level (SF-APPS-085).
Half-to-half PPP changes are susceptible to artifacts (e.g., free throw spikes) and confounds that can mimic or obscure real effects (SF15, SF-APPS-018).
Small sample sizes and measurement noise often lead to inconclusive results for advanced on-off metrics (SF-APPS-018).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether a defense's effect on opponent H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait has not been directly tested.
The degree of year-to-year stability of any such team-level metric remains unknown.
The specific sample size and power needed to detect a team-level defensive H2-H1 trait in NBA data have not been determined.
own_inferences: Given the noise in single-game half-to-half PPP differences, aggregating to a season-level metric still requires many games to overcome measurement error; with only 120 team-seasons, year-to-year reliability tests will be underpowered unless the true signal is very strong.
Confounding by game script (score margin, end-of-quarter tactics, lineup changes, garbage time) can induce team-level patterns in H2-H1 change that may be mistaken for a defensive trait.
The low reliability of a conceptually similar player-level half-to-half metric warns that attenuation is likely for this team-level measure, making it difficult to establish a stable trait.
uncertainties: The true inter-team variance in defensive H2-H1 suppression is unknown; it could be large enough to overcome expected measurement noise.
The reliability of the metric over a full 82-game season may be higher than player-level half-to-half reliability, but the magnitude is not yet estimated.
Novel adjustments for opponent strength and game script could reduce confounds, but their effectiveness and validity remain uncertain without pilot testing.

historical_effect.explanation: The retrieval returned records showing that similarly motivated half-to-half derived metrics exhibited low measurement reliability and were often untestable or artifact-ridden. This evidence shifted the assessment toward a high risk of untestability and led to a recommendation not to proceed, whereas without it one might have assumed a simple reliability design could work.

blocking_constraints.text: Half-to-half change in opponent points per possession is a noisy metric per game; aggregating over a season may still yield low reliability if underlying trait effect is small, as historical player-level evidence suggests.
Only 120 team-seasons across 4 seasons; a year-to-year correlation test would have about 90 paired observations, giving low power to detect a weak reliability (e.g., ICC<0.25).
Game script (score margin, end-of-quarter strategies, garbage time) affects second-half possession quality, potentially creating spurious defensive signals that are not a stable team trait.

prior_work.summary: No retrieved study directly tested the reliability of a team-level defensive opponent H2-H1 change trait. Indirect evidence from player-level half-to-half metrics and artifact-prone PPP change studies provides context but does not answer the question.

risks.text: Single-game H2-H1 PPP differences have high variance; a full-season average may still be unreliable if underlying signal is weak.
120 team-seasons and ~90 paired year-to-year observations provide insufficient power to detect a small-to-moderate reliability coefficient.
Game script confounds (score differential at half, opponent tactics, rotations) are difficult to fully adjust and may persist as spurious team effects.
If teams are selected by extreme H2-H1 values, regression to the mean may create illusory instability across seasons.
If the true between-team variance in H2-H1 suppression is near zero, the metric will inherently be unreliable.
Testing multiple operationalizations or slice-and-dice subgroups without correction inflates the false positive rate.
Rule changes, playing style trends, and season-specific fatigue/scheduling could alter the defensive trait across seasons, undermining year-to-year stability.

design.estimand: Season-level Spearman-Brown corrected reliability of a team's average opponent second-half minus first-half points per possession (PPP), adjusted for pre-game opponent offensive rating and in-game score differential at half.
design.sample: All 120 team-seasons from 2022-23 through 2025-26. For split‑half reliability, each team's games within a season are randomly partitioned into two halves (balanced on home/away and opponent strength). For year‑to‑year stability, pair consecutive seasons for the same team (max 90 pairs).
design.power: Split‑half: if true full-season ICC=0.2, half-season Spearman-Brown-corrected estimate would require ~400 team-seasons for 80% power, far exceeding available data. Year‑over‑year correlation: 90 pairs can detect r=0.29 at 80% power, but a weak trait (r<0.2) would be undetectable.
design.controls: Adjust opponent H2-H1 PPP by subtracting the same opponent's average H2-H1 PPP in all non-garbage games (or use a mixed model). Include a non‑linear function of half-time score margin (e.g., restricted cubic spline) to account for game script. Exclude possessions classified as garbage time (last 5 minutes, 20+ point margin).
design.falsification: Test whether the team's own H2-H1 offensive PPP change shows similar reliability; a genuine defensive trait should not symmetrically appear on offense. Placebo test: randomly shuffle opponent assignments to break defensive pairings and confirm zero reliability.
design.multiplicity: Pre‑register a single primary metric: Spearman-Brown corrected split‑half reliability of adjusted opponent H2-H1 PPP change. No unplanned subgroup analyses; if explored, apply Holm-Bonferroni correction.
design.decision_rule: Conclude the trait is reliable if the corrected reliability coefficient exceeds 0.5 and its 95% CI lower bound exceeds 0.3. If the raw split-half correlation is <0.2, declare the test underpowered and interpret results as inconclusive.
design.data_version: NBA stats API play-by-play data as of 2026-10-06, processed into half-level PPP using derived play‑type possession records.

Research question (as posed on 2026-10-06, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 120 team-seasons

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

{"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["defensive suppression", "opponent H2-H1 change", "second-half scoring decline", "team defensive trait", "reliability"], "methodological_questions": ["reliability estimation", "year-to-year stability", "confounding by game script", "sample size requirements", "measurement error in half-by-half splits"], "query": "Is a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change a reliable team trait?"}}

reasoning_details.text:
We are asked to produce only the retrieval call in stage 1. We need to identify research concepts and methodological questions from the research question: "A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait." The area is defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid). H2-H1 change likely means the difference in performance or scoring between the second half and first half. So the concept is about defenses forcing opponents to score less in the second half relative to the first, as a persistent team ability.

Research concepts might include: defensive suppression, second-half adjustment, opponent scoring decline, team trait reliability, H2-H1 change. Methodological questions: reliability measurement (e.g., intraclass correlation, split-half, year-to-year stability), confounding by opponent offense adjustments, game script effects (e.g., blowouts, pace), sample size, measurement error in H2-H1 change, selection bias (only certain games where defense actually played), and regression to the mean.

So for the retrieval, we need to query for related past studies in this project. Let's craft concepts and questions.

Concepts: "defensive suppression", "opponent second-half scoring decline", "H2-H1 change", "team defensive trait", "reliability".

Methodological questions: "reliability estimation", "year-to-year stability", "confounding by game script", "sample size requirements", "measurement error in half-by-half splits".

Query: something like "Is a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change a reliable team trait?"

We'll output that.

We need to process the retrieval result and follow steps 4-9. Retrieval returned 4 records: FAM:SF-APPS-085, FAM:SF-APPS-018, FAM:SF15, FAM:SF-APPS-068. None of them directly address the question "A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait." But we need to extract relevant historical evidence, failed approaches, etc. We must also use read_family if needed for more details (but may not need; the document snippets are sufficient for most). We'll first list research concepts and methodological questions already identified in Stage 1. Then historical_evidence: for each returned record, we note the id, status as recorded (auto_outcome_status), and a finding summary. failed_approaches: we can note approaches that failed or limitations that are relevant. But the question is about reliability of team trait. The closest records: FAM:SF-APPS-085 is about split-half reliability of a player attribute, not a team trait; it shows low measure reliability for a derived metric (Connector quality Q_p). That might indicate that measure reliability is a general issue for such advanced metrics, but not directly about this defense H2-H1 change. FAM:SF-APPS-018 is about playsheet ranking validation, involving half-to-half PPP change but not team-level reliability; it notes issues like leakage, low measurement reliability, small sample. FAM:SF15 is about foul-trouble sequencing, not relevant. FAM:SF-APPS-068 is about PCI artifact, not relevant. So no direct prior work on the reliability of defense effect on opponent H2-H1 change as a team trait. So prior_work.already_answered: unknown or no? The records are not answering the question. We'll say unknown because no directly relevant study retrieved. But we can say that it hasn't been answered. I'll set already_answered: unknown, and cited empty.

Now we need to assess testability: p_testable based on data and methodological risks. Data has 120 team-seasons (30 teams * 4 seasons? Actually 2022-23 to 2025-26, four full seasons except 2025-26 regular season complete from 2026-04-13, but they said data available includes all those seasons and playoffs. So 4 seasons * 30 teams = 120 team-seasons. So we have 120 observations of team-season. The research question: "A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait." We need to define the measure: For each team-season, we could compute the average change in opponent's offensive rating (or PPP) from first half to second half when that team is on defense. But this could be confounded by game script, opponent strength, etc. The question is whether that effect is a reliable team trait, i.e., stable across seasons for the same team (or across halves within season?), presumably year-to-year reliability. So we need to test the intraclass correlation or split-half reliability or correlation between team-level effect in one season and the next, or correlation between first half of season and second half. But we need to account for sample size: only 120 team-seasons. If we compute year-to-year correlation for 30 teams over 4 years, we have limited power. Alternatively, we could compute split-half reliability within a season by splitting games, but then each team's measure would be noisy due to limited games (half a season ~41 games per team, opponent H2-H1 change may have high variance). So measurement error is a big issue. The retrieved record FAM:SF-APPS-085 shows that a player-level metric with n=102 had low reliability (ICC 0.216). That suggests that derived metrics like this might have low reliability, but at team level with more possessions it might be higher. Still, we need to consider risks: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, CONFOUNDING (game script, lead/loss, rotation changes, garbage time), RTM_SELECTION if we condition on game situations, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD (if we use data that includes future performance to define metric, but half-by-half is within game so not lookahead). OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL: the outcome is H2-H1 change, which is derived from play-by-play, but that's fine. MECHANICAL_FLOOR? Possibly if teams that trail more in H2 due to their defense being poor, but H2-H1 change could be influenced by score effects. BASE_RATE: if few teams have large changes, distribution may be narrow. MULTIPLE_TESTING if we test many metrics. DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY: rule changes, season trends could affect year-to-year stability. LABEL_ERROR: misclassification of defensive responsibility? But we are using team defense, so opponent half-court offense against that team's defense. Not an issue.

Now, p_testable: I'd say moderate probability that question can be answered with useful power, but with many risks. I might put 0.4 because sample size and noise could make it hard to detect reliability if effect size is small. But we can make a design with careful normalization. I'll set p_testable = 0.4. block constraints: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER (only 120 team-seasons, year-to-year reliability needs many seasons), MEASURE_RELIABILITY (H2-H1 change per game is noisy, requiring many games), CONFOUNDING (game script). Also multiple testing if we look at many variations.

Risks: list those.

Predicted outcome probabilities: need to guess what a competent test would conclude. I think it's likely that any signal would be weak and may end up untestable or rejected due to insufficient reliability. So I'd assign: supported low (0.1), rejected 0.2, untestable 0.4, artifact 0.1, uncertain 0.2. But that's subjective. I'll set based on historical evidence of measure reliability issues.

Decision: proceed_with_changes? Or do_not_proceed? I lean do_not_proceed because sample size is limited (only 120 team-seasons, and need at least two seasons per team for reliability, so ~60 teams to correlate) and the measure is likely noisy, and historical evidence suggests similar advanced metrics suffer from low reliability. However, one could attempt with split-half within season and Spearman-Brown correction, but still need to control confounds. So I'd recommend do_not_proceed unless they can increase sample size with more seasons or use a better methodology. But the task says "Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data... and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed." So minimum required sample size for 80% power to detect a correlation of 0.3 (considered moderate) would require ~85 pairs (n=85), which we'd have 90 pairs. But if true correlation is small (0.15), power would be low. So sample size is borderline. We could also use split-half reliability within a season by randomly splitting games, then apply Spearman-Brown to estimate reliability for full season. That would give 120 observations, but each split half's measure would be based on ~41 games, which might be noisy leading to attenuation. That's where measurement error could make it untestable. Historical evidence (FAM:SF-APPS-085) shows that with 102 players split-half reliability was 0.215, leading to low ICC. So similar attenuation likely for team-level if underlying stability is modest.

So do_not_proceed is reasonable, but the design can be presented.

We need to process the retrieval result and follow steps 4-9. Retrieval returned 4 records: FAM:SF-APPS-085, FAM:SF-APPS-018, FAM:SF15, FAM:SF-APPS-068. None of them directly address the question "A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait." But we need to extract relevant historical evidence, failed approaches, etc. We must also use read_family if needed for more details (but may not need; the document snippets are sufficient for most). We'll first list research concepts and methodological questions already identified in Stage 1. Then historical_evidence: for each returned record, we note the id, status as recorded (auto_outcome_status), and a finding summary. failed_approaches: we can note approaches that failed or limitations that are relevant. But the question is about reliability of team trait. The closest records: FAM:SF-APPS-085 is about split-half reliability of a player attribute, not a team trait; it shows low measure reliability for a derived metric (Connector quality Q_p). That might indicate that measure reliability is a general issue for such advanced metrics, but not directly about this defense H2-H1 change. FAM:SF-APPS-018 is about playsheet ranking validation, involving half-to-half PPP change but not team-level reliability; it notes issues like leakage, low measurement reliability, small sample. FAM:SF15 is about foul-trouble sequencing, not relevant. FAM:SF-APPS-068 is about PCI artifact, not relevant. So no direct prior work on the reliability of defense effect on opponent H2-H1 change as a team trait. So prior_work.already_answered: unknown or no? The records are not answering the question. We'll say unknown because no directly relevant study retrieved. But we can say that it hasn't been answered. I'll set already_answered: unknown, and cited empty.

Now we need to assess testability: p_testable based on data and methodological risks. Data has 120 team-seasons (30 teams * 4 seasons? Actually 2022-23 to 2025-26, four full seasons except 2025-26 regular season complete from 2026-04-13, but they said data available includes all those seasons and playoffs. So 4 seasons * 30 teams = 120 team-seasons. So we have 120 observations of team-season. The research question: "A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait." We need to define the measure: For each team-season, we could compute the average change in opponent's offensive rating (or PPP) from first half to second half when that team is on defense. But this could be confounded by game script, opponent strength, etc. The question is whether that effect is a reliable team trait, i.e., stable across seasons for the same team (or across halves within season?), presumably year-to-year reliability. So we need to test the intraclass correlation or split-half reliability or correlation between team-level effect in one season and the next, or correlation between first half of season and second half. But we need to account for sample size: only 120 team-seasons. If we compute year-to-year correlation for 30 teams over 4 years, we have limited power. Alternatively, we could compute split-half reliability within a season by splitting games, but then each team's measure would be noisy due to limited games (half a season ~41 games per team, opponent H2-H1 change may have high variance). So measurement error is a big issue. The retrieved record FAM:SF-APPS-085 shows that a player-level metric with n=102 had low reliability (ICC 0.216). That suggests that derived metrics like this might have low reliability, but at team level with more possessions it might be higher. Still, we need to consider risks: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, CONFOUNDING (game script, lead/loss, rotation changes, garbage time), RTM_SELECTION if we condition on game situations, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD (if we use data that includes future performance to define metric, but half-by-half is within game so not lookahead). OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL: the outcome is H2-H1 change, which is derived from play-by-play, but that's fine. MECHANICAL_FLOOR? Possibly if teams that trail more in H2 due to their defense being poor, but H2-H1 change could be influenced by score effects. BASE_RATE: if few teams have large changes, distribution may be narrow. MULTIPLE_TESTING if we test many metrics. DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY: rule changes, season trends could affect year-to-year stability. LABEL_ERROR: misclassification of defensive responsibility? But we are using team defense, so opponent half-court offense against that team's defense. Not an issue.

Now, p_testable: I'd say moderate probability that question can be answered with useful power, but with many risks. I might put 0.4 because sample size and noise could make it hard to detect reliability if effect size is small. But we can make a design with careful normalization. I'll set p_testable = 0.4. block constraints: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER (only 120 team-seasons, year-to-year reliability needs many seasons), MEASURE_RELIABILITY (H2-H1 change per game is noisy, requiring many games), CONFOUNDING (game script). Also multiple testing if we look at many variations.

Risks: list those.

Predicted outcome probabilities: need to guess what a competent test would conclude. I think it's likely that any signal would be weak and may end up untestable or rejected due to insufficient reliability. So I'd assign: supported low (0.1), rejected 0.2, untestable 0.4, artifact 0.1, uncertain 0.2. But that's subjective. I'll set based on historical evidence of measure reliability issues.

Decision: proceed_with_changes? Or do_not_proceed? I lean do_not_proceed because sample size is limited (only 120 team-seasons, and need at least two seasons per team for reliability, so ~60 teams to correlate) and the measure is likely noisy, and historical evidence suggests similar advanced metrics suffer from low reliability. However, one could attempt with split-half within season and Spearman-Brown correction, but still need to control confounds. So I'd recommend do_not_proceed unless they can increase sample size with more seasons or use a better methodology. But the task says "Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data... and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed." So I will output do_not_proceed, but still provide a design as required.

Design: would need to define estimand: "year-to-year Pearson correlation (or ICC) of team-level average opponent H2-H1 PPP change (adjusted for game-script confounds)." unit: team-season. sample: all 120 team-seasons from 2022-23 to 2025-26, but test reliability by correlating season i with i+1, using paired observations (30 teams * 3 pairs = 90), not enough power for small effects. So minimum required sample size for 80% power to detect a correlation of 0.3 (considered moderate) would require ~85 pairs (n=85), which we'd have 90 pairs. But if true correlation is small (0.15), power would be low. So sample size is borderline. We could also use split-half reliability within a season by randomly splitting games, then apply Spearman-Brown to estimate reliability for full season. That would give 120 observations, but each split half's measure would be based on ~41 games, which might be noisy leading to attenuation. That's where measurement error could make it untestable. Historical evidence (FAM:SF-APPS-085) shows that with 102 players split-half reliability was 0.215, leading to low ICC. So similar attenuation likely for team-level if underlying stability is modest.

So do_not_proceed is reasonable, but the design can be presented.

evidence_establishes: from these records, we learn that derived half-to-half metrics can have low reliability (SF-APPS-085), and that half-to-half changes are susceptible to artifacts and confounds (SF15, SF-APPS-018). Also that sample size constraints limit power for detecting stable traits. So it's not directly established for this team-level trait, but relevant evidence of challenges.

evidence_does_not_establish: whether a defense's effect on opponent H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait; no study directly tested this.

own_inferences: "Given the noise in half-to-half scoring changes at the single-game level, aggregating to team-season will require many games to overcome measurement error; with 120 team-seasons, year-to-year reliability tests have limited power. Confounding by game script (e.g., blowouts, end-of-quarter strategies, lineup changes) may induce spurious team-level patterns. The historical low reliability of derived player metrics warns that similar attenuation may affect team-level H2-H1 metrics, making it unlikely to find a stable trait without strong signal."
